note: Frozen identical-student A/B test script (Groq vs Gemini). 3 physics + 3 chemistry + 4 english = 10 concepts, per owner instruction to exclude biology. All misconception/correctTyped/wrongTyped/offTopic text is copied verbatim (or trivially reworded to first person for `misconception`) from this repo's own educational-brain/ and src/lib/teaching/assets/ seed sources — nothing invented. Provenance is cited per field.

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think rubbing makes the charge appear out of nothing.
concepts.misconceptionSource: educational-brain/concepts/physics/phys.em.electric-charge.md#Misconceptions M1, reworded to first person from 'Rubbing makes the electrons appear.'
concepts.correctTyped: Still exactly zero — the cloth is now +40e, because rubbing only TRANSFERS electrons from one surface to the other. Charge is conserved, never manufactured.
concepts.correctTypedSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/authoredSeedAssets.ts, phys.em.electric-charge mcq probe, isCorrect choice text (verbatim)
concepts.wrongTyped: About -40e — the rubbing generated new charge on the rod.
concepts.offTopic: A 4 kg box on a level floor starts to slide only when a horizontal push exceeds 20 N. What is the coefficient of static friction? (g = 10 m/s^2)
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/authoredSeedAssets.ts, phys.mech.friction short_answer probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think the normal force always equals the object's weight, no matter what.
concepts.correctTyped: 20 N — static friction matches the push, up to its 40 N ceiling.
concepts.wrongTyped: 40 N — static friction always equals mu_s times N.
concepts.wrongTypedSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/authoredSeedAssets.ts, same probe, choice tagged phys.mech.friction:MC-STATIC-ALWAYS-MAX (verbatim, mu_s spelled out for plain text)
concepts.offTopic: A book rests on a table. Earth's gravity pulls the book down. What is the Third-Law reaction to that force?
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/authoredSeedAssets.ts, phys.mech.newtons-third-law mcq probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)

concepts.subject: physics
concepts.misconception: I think the heavier object pushes harder in a collision.
concepts.correctTyped: Exactly equal in size, opposite in direction — the bicycle just accelerates far more.
concepts.wrongTyped: The lorry exerts a much larger force because it is heavier and moving.
concepts.offTopic: A rubber rod rubbed with fur ends up with charge -40e. What is the charge on the fur?
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/authoredSeedAssets.ts, phys.em.electric-charge mcq probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)

concepts.subject: chemistry
concepts.misconception: I think the mole is a mass — it's like a gram.
concepts.correctTyped: No — 18g water = 1 mol (molar mass 18), 18g glucose = 0.1 mol (molar mass 180). Same mass, very different number of molecules.
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — same mass means same number of molecules for any substance.
concepts.offTopic: For the reaction N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, if you start with 1 mol N2 and 2 mol H2, what is the limiting reagent?
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/chemistrySeedAssets.ts, chem.found.stoichiometry mcq probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)

concepts.subject: chemistry
concepts.misconception: I think the coefficient 2 in a formula means 2 grams, not 2 moles.
concepts.misconceptionSource: educational-brain/concepts/chemistry/chem.found.stoichiometry.md#Misconceptions MC-1, characteristic phrase adapted to first person from 'The coefficient 2 in 2H2 looks like 2 grams of H2.'
concepts.correctTyped: Coefficients represent MOLES (or molecules), not grams — 2 means 2 moles of Mg (= 48.6g), not 2g.
concepts.wrongTyped: Nothing wrong — coefficients directly give the mass in grams.
concepts.offTopic: Water (H2O) has a relatively low boiling point (100C) compared to many ionic compounds. Does this mean the O-H covalent bonds within water molecules are weak?
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/chemistrySeedAssets.ts, chem.bond.covalent-bonding mcq probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)

concepts.subject: chemistry
concepts.misconception: I think CO2 must be polar because it has polar C=O bonds.
concepts.misconceptionSource: educational-brain/concepts/chemistry/chem.bond.covalent-bonding.md#Misconceptions MC-1, characteristic phrase reworded to first person from 'CO2 is a polar molecule because it contains polar C=O bonds.'
concepts.correctTyped: No — linear symmetry cancels the dipoles; compare bent water.
concepts.wrongTyped: Yes — it has two very polar bonds, and a molecule with polar bonds is a polar molecule.
concepts.offTopic: Which contains more molecules: 2g of H2 (molar mass 2 g/mol) or 32g of O2 (molar mass 32 g/mol)?
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/chemistrySeedAssets.ts, chem.found.mole-concept mcq probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)

concepts.subject: english
concepts.misconception: I think pronouns can only replace people, not things.
concepts.correctTypedSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/englishProbeBatch2.ts, eng.grammar.pronouns mcq probe, isCorrect choice text (verbatim)
concepts.wrongTyped: Nothing — "it" only replaces people, and "book" is not a person, so this must be a different kind of word.
concepts.offTopic: In "She IS happy," is anything physically moving? Is "is" still a verb?
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/englishProbeBatch3.ts, eng.grammar.verbs mcq probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)

concepts.subject: english
concepts.misconception: I think a verb has to show physical action, so "is" and "know" can't really be verbs.
concepts.correctTyped: Nothing is physically moving, but "is" is still a verb — it connects the subject to a state or description.
concepts.correctTypedSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/englishProbeBatch3.ts, eng.grammar.verbs mcq probe, isCorrect choice text (verbatim)
concepts.wrongTyped: "Is" cannot be a verb since nothing is physically moving.
concepts.offTopic: In "The child seems happy," is "happy" an adjective?
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/englishProbeBatch1.ts, eng.grammar.adjectives mcq probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)

concepts.subject: english
concepts.misconception: I think adjectives always have to come right before the noun.
concepts.correctTyped: Yes — a predicate adjective after the linking verb "seems," describing "child".
concepts.correctTypedSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/englishProbeBatch1.ts, eng.grammar.adjectives mcq probe, isCorrect choice text (verbatim)
concepts.wrongTyped: No — adjectives must come directly before the noun they describe.
concepts.offTopic: In "The meeting is at 3pm," what relationship does "at" express?
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/authoredSeedAssets.ts, eng.grammar.prepositions mcq probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)

concepts.subject: english
concepts.misconception: I think prepositions only ever show where something is.
concepts.correctTyped: Time — prepositions cover time, means, and other relationships, not just location.
concepts.correctTypedSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/authoredSeedAssets.ts, eng.grammar.prepositions mcq probe, isCorrect choice text (verbatim)
concepts.wrongTyped: Location — prepositions always show where something is.
concepts.offTopic: In "I bought a book. IT was expensive," what does "it" replace?
concepts.offTopicSource: src/lib/teaching/assets/englishProbeBatch2.ts, eng.grammar.pronouns mcq probe stem (verbatim, different concept, same subject)
